analysis.one_liner: Makes pre-dispute nondisclosure and nondisparagement clauses unenforceable in sexual assault and harassment cases.
analysis.headline: The House Judiciary Committee approved the bill 22–13, but it never received a vote by the full House before that Congress ended in January 2023.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would void contracts' pre-dispute clauses that require workers or consumers to stay silent about sexual assault or sexual harassment. Before any dispute arises, a signed nondisclosure or nondisparagement clause could not be enforced in court in a case alleging conduct that broke federal, state, or tribal law. Post-dispute settlement agreements—signed after a claim exists—would still be allowed.
analysis.who_benefits: Workers and, in some cases, consumers who had signed broad nondisclosure or nondisparagement clauses before any dispute arose. Because the findings note that 87 to 94 percent of people who experience sexual harassment never file a formal complaint, the main beneficiaries are employees—disproportionately women—who would be free to speak publicly about assault or harassment without breaching a contract they signed as a condition of the job.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Workers and harassment survivors bound by NDAs

how_it_helps.text: Bars courts from enforcing pre-dispute nondisclosure or nondisparagement clauses in disputes involving sexual assault or sexual harassment, wherever the alleged conduct would violate federal, tribal, or state law [S2][S3].

The bill's findings state that one in three women faces workplace sexual harassment during her career and that an estimated 87 to 94 percent of those who experience it never file a formal complaint; lifting pre-dispute silencing clauses is aimed at letting survivors come forward [S3].
The ban reaches clauses signed by employees, contractors, and consumers alike, not just traditional employment agreements [S3].
It preserves state laws on pseudonyms in filings and does not override stronger state protections, and it applies only to claims filed on or after enactment [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Employers that rely on pre-dispute NDAs and nondisparagement clauses lose a tool for keeping alleged misconduct out of public view, and people accused of assault or harassment lose contractual protection against being named. Legitimate settlements remain possible—parties can still agree to confidentiality after a dispute exists—but the initial leverage of a contract signed before any dispute would be gone.

drawbacks.text: The bill leaves post-dispute nondisclosure agreements fully enforceable, so a settlement reached after a claim is filed can still require silence, meaning money can still buy confidentiality once a dispute exists [S3].

It does not touch pre-dispute arbitration clauses themselves; a worker could still be routed into private arbitration, where the Speak Out Act's assumption of a public judicial forum does not apply [S3].

Critics of limiting NDAs argue that some employees value confidential resolution and that broad confidentiality helps both sides settle quickly; this bill removes that pre-committed option even when both parties would have wanted it.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The cost side is narrow: employers and accused individuals lose the ability to enforce silence clauses signed before a dispute, while ordinary settlement freedom after a dispute is untouched. The benefit—restoring survivors' ability to speak about assault and harassment and deterring repeat misconduct by making it harder to hide—clearly outweighs that cost for most workers. The main honest caveat is that the bill is deliberately modest: it does not reach arbitration or post-dispute settlements, so it is a partial fix, not a ban on confidential settlements.

outcome.mechanism: The bill cleared the House Judiciary Committee on a 22–13 vote in July 2022 but never came up for a vote by the full House before the Congress ended on January 3, 2023.

narrative.text: Representative Lois Frankel of Florida introduced the bill on June 24, 2022, with six original cosponsors, including two Republicans (Reps. Ken Buck and Morgan Griffith) [S3].
The bill was referred to the House Judiciary Committee the day it was introduced [S5].
On July 13, 2022, the committee held a markup and ordered the bill reported with amendments by a vote of 22–13 [S5].
No further action appears in the record; the bill never received a vote by the full House, and it expired when the 117th Congress ended on January 3, 2023 [S5].
The bill would have made pre-dispute nondisclosure and nondisparagement clauses judicially unenforceable in sexual assault and sexual harassment disputes [S2][S3].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Employers with pre-dispute NDAs kept a tool this bill would have taken away, since the House never voted. In practice, workers did not end the year worse off on this issue: Congress passed an identical Senate companion bill, which the President signed into law in December 2022, making the policy itself law even though this House bill never reached the floor.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Employers relying on NDAs—though the Senate version became law

industries.industry: Employers that use pre-dispute NDAs and nondisparagement clauses
industries.note: The bill removes their ability to enforce contracts signed before any dispute that require workers or customers to stay silent about sexual assault or harassment allegations. That silencing tool was central to keeping such disputes out of public view, so its interest runs against the workers the bill protects.
